{{Short description|none}}
This is a list of things named after the English mathematician [[John Horton Conway]] (1937–2020). 

* [[Conway algebra]] – an algebraic structure introduced by Paweł Traczyk and [[Józef H. Przytycki]]<ref>[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/230815149_Conway_type_invariants_of_links_and_Kauffman's_method Conway type invariants of links and Kauffman's method] by [[Jozef H. Przytycki]]</ref>
* [[Conway's base 13 function]] – a function used as a counterexample to the converse of the [[intermediate value theorem]]<ref>Oman, Greg (2014). [https://www.uccs.edu/Documents/goman/Converse%20of%20IVT.pdf "The Converse of the Intermediate Value Theorem: From Conway to Cantor to Cosets and Beyond"] Missouri J. Math. Sci. 26 (2): 134–150</ref>
* [[Conway chained arrow notation]] – a notation for expressing certain extremely large numbers<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.greatplay.net/essays/large-numbers-part-ii-graham-and-conway|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130625000516/http://www.greatplay.net/essays/large-numbers-part-ii-graham-and-conway|url-status=dead|archive-date=2013-06-25|title=Large Numbers, Part 2: Graham and Conway – Greatplay.net|date=2013-06-25|work=archive.is|access-date=2018-02-18}}</ref>
*[[Conway circle]] – a geometrical construction based on extending the sides of a triangle<ref>{{Cite web|title=John Horton Conway|url=http://www.cardcolm.org/JHC.html|website=www.cardcolm.org|access-date=2020-05-29}}</ref>
* [[Conway criterion]] – a criterion for identifying [[prototile]]s that admit a periodic tiling<ref>''Will It Tile? Try the Conway Criterion!'' by [[Doris Schattschneider]] [[Mathematics Magazine]] Vol. 53, No. 4 (Sep., 1980), pp. 224-233</ref>
* [[Conway group]] – any of the groups [[Leech lattice#Symmetries|Co<sub>0</sub>]], [[Conway group Co1|Co<sub>1</sub>]], [[Conway group Co2|Co<sub>2</sub>]], or [[Conway group Co3|Co<sub>3</sub>]]<ref name=groups>''Sphere packings, lattices, and groups'' (with Neil Sloane). Springer-Verlag, New York, Series: Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften, 290, {{ISBN|9780387966175}}</ref>
* [[Conway group Co1|Conway group Co<sub>1</sub>]] – one of the [[sporadic simple group]]s discovered by Conway in 1968<ref name=groups/>
* [[Conway group Co2|Conway group Co<sub>2</sub>]] – one of the sporadic simple groups discovered by Conway in 1968<ref name=groups/>
* [[Conway group Co3|Conway group Co<sub>3</sub>]] – one of the sporadic simple groups discovered by Conway in 1968<ref name=groups/>
* [[Conway knot]] – a curious knot having the same Alexander polynomial and Conway polynomial as the unknot
* [[Conway notation (knot theory)]] – a notation invented by Conway for describing knots in [[knot theory]]<ref name=knot>{{Citation|first=John Horton|last=Conway|author-link=John Horton Conway|chapter=An enumeration of knots and links, and some of their algebraic properties|publisher=Pergamon|year=1970|pages=329–358|title=Computational Problems in Abstract Algebra |oclc=322649 |isbn=978-0080129754}}</ref>
* [[Conway polyhedron notation]] – notation invented by Conway used to describe polyhedra<ref name=biblio/>
* [[Conway polynomial (finite fields)]] – an irreducible polynomial used in finite field theory<ref name=biblio/>
* [[Conway puzzle]] – a packing problem invented by Conway using rectangular blocks<ref name=genius/>
* [[Conway sphere]] – a [[N-sphere|2-sphere]] intersecting a given knot in the 3-sphere or [[Ball (mathematics)|3-ball]] [[Transversality (mathematics)|transversely]] in four points<ref name=knot/>
* [[Conway triangle notation]] – notation which allows trigonometric functions of a triangle to be managed algebraically<ref name=biblio>[http://www.math.princeton.edu/WebCV/ConwayBIB.pdf Bibliography of John H. Conway] Mathematics Department, Princeton University (2009)</ref>
* [[Conway's 99-graph problem]] – a problem invented by Conway asking if a certain undirected graph exists<ref>[https://mathoverflow.net/q/162583 A question related to Conways 99 graph problem] [[MathOverflow]]</ref>
* [[Conway sequence]] – a self-referential sequence in which each term describes the digits of the previous term
* [[Conway's constant]] – a constant used in the study of the [[Look-and-say sequence]]<ref name=sequence>Conway, J.H. and Guy, R.K. "The Look and Say Sequence." In ''The Book of Numbers''. New York: Springer-Verlag, pp. 208-209, 1996.</ref>
* [[Conway's dead fly problem]] – does there exist a [[Danzer set]] whose points are separated at a bounded distance from each other?<ref>{{citation
 | last = Roberts | first = Siobhan | authorlink = Siobhan Roberts
 | isbn = 978-1-62040-593-2
 | location = New York
 | mr = 3329687
 | page = 382
 | publisher = Bloomsbury Press
 | title = Genius at Play: The Curious Mind of John Horton Conway
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=gJssCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA382
 | year = 2015}}</ref>
* [[Conway's Game of Life]] – a cellular automaton defined on the two-dimensional orthogonal grid of square cells<ref name=genius>[[Michael Harris (mathematician)|Harris, Michael]] (2015). [http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v523/n7561/full/523406a.html Review of ''Genius At Play: The Curious Mind of John Horton Conway''] ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', 23 July 2015</ref>
* [[Conway's Soldiers]] – a one-person mathematical game resembling [[peg solitaire]]<ref name=games>Berlekamp, E.R.; Conway, J.H; and Guy, R.K. "The Solitaire Army." In ''[[Winning Ways for Your Mathematical Plays]]'', Vol. 2: Academic Press, pp. 715-717 and 729, 1982.</ref>
* [[Conway's thrackle conjecture]] – In graph theory, the conjecture that no [[thrackle]] has more edges than vertices
* [[Alexander–Conway polynomial]] – a knot invariant which assigns a polynomial to each knot type in [[knot theory]]<ref name=knot/>
